F01-01.F01-01-d1: It buys higher placement for chosen pages through Google's paid listings.
F01-01.F01-01-d2: It sets the ranking position of each page by submitting its target keywords to Google.
F01-01.F01-01-d3: It is a technical layer that can raise rankings on its own, whatever the content quality.

F01-02.F01-02-d1: Most changes take effect within two days, so judge results after 48 hours.
F01-02.F01-02-d2: Effects typically wait for the next core update, so judge results after that rollout.
F01-02.F01-02-d3: Google applies changes on a fixed six-month cycle, so evaluate them twice a year.

F01-03.F01-03-d1: A sitemap is required for indexing, since links alone don't let Google index pages.
F01-03.F01-03-d2: A sitemap mainly boosts rankings, so sites without one usually rank lower.
F01-03.F01-03-d3: Small sites need one to rank, while large sites can rely on links.

F01-04.F01-04-d1: Open the page in your own browser and check that every section loads.
F01-04.F01-04-d2: Run the HTML through a markup validator, since valid code shows Google can read it.
F01-04.F01-04-d3: View Google's cached copy of the page, which shows the version Googlebot rendered.

F01-05.F01-05-d1: Keywords in folder names give each page in that directory a ranking boost.
F01-05.F01-05-d2: Directories pass more PageRank to their pages than links in the navigation do.
F01-05.F01-05-d3: It gives each folder its own authority score, separate from the domain.

F01-06.F01-06-d1: Duplicate product URLs trigger a manual action once they pass a set share of the site.
F01-06.F01-06-d2: They can lead to a duplicate content penalty that lowers the whole domain.
F01-06.F01-06-d3: They trigger a penalty unless each one has a canonical tag.

F01-07.F01-07-d1: Use a redirect when both URLs need to stay accessible to visitors.
F01-07.F01-07-d2: Use a redirect when the pages differ in content, and a canonical when both URLs match.
F01-07.F01-07-d3: Use a canonical when users should land on the preferred URL, since it forwards them.

F01-08.F01-08-d1: Include each variation at least once, since Google matches exact strings.
F01-08.F01-08-d2: Repeat the main phrase at a 2-3% density so Google ranks each variant.
F01-08.F01-08-d3: Create a separate page for each variation so every phrasing has its own match.

F01-09.F01-09-d1: Google shows them as written unless they exceed the pixel limit.
F01-09.F01-09-d2: Titles may be rewritten, but a meta description is shown whenever the page has one.
F01-09.F01-09-d3: Google uses them as written once the page has enough authority to be trusted.

F01-10.F01-10-d1: Compressed images with the target keyword repeated in each alt text.
F01-10.F01-10-d2: Images placed in a separate gallery, with file names that match the main keyword.
F01-10.F01-10-d3: Large images with keyword captions, since Google can't read alt text.

F01-11.F01-11-d1: Embed it in a long article where it supports the text as a secondary element.
F01-11.F01-11-d2: Host it on YouTube and link to it, since Google can't index self-hosted video.
F01-11.F01-11-d3: Place several videos on one page so Google sees it as a stronger video hub.

F01-12.F01-12-d1: Add nofollow to all external links so your pages keep their PageRank.
F01-12.F01-12-d2: Only links to competitors need nofollow, since they could pass them authority.
F01-12.F01-12-d3: Paid links can stay as normal links if the sponsor is relevant to the topic.

F01-13.F01-13-d1: An exact-match domain is still a strong signal, and .com ranks best worldwide.
F01-13.F01-13-d2: A .com domain usually outranks country-code domains, even for local searches.
F01-13.F01-13-d3: Keywords in the domain can lift rankings, while TLD choice has no geographic effect.

F01-14.F01-14-d1: About 1,500 words with an H2 every 300 words ranks best.
F01-14.F01-14-d2: Longer pages usually rank higher, so aim to beat top results on length.
F01-14.F01-14-d3: Google prefers one H1 and at least three H2s, whatever the length.

F01-15.F01-15-d1: It was retired years ago and no longer plays a role.
F01-15.F01-15-d2: It is the main ranking system, with other signals as tie-breakers.
F01-15.F01-15-d3: It still exists but only affects crawling, not the ranking system.

F01-16.F01-16-d1: Running Google Ads can lift organic rankings for the same keywords.
F01-16.F01-16-d2: Ad campaigns can buy faster crawling, but not rankings.
F01-16.F01-16-d3: Promotion spend counts as a brand signal that Google feeds into rankings.

F01-17.F01-17-d1: Wait for the next core update, since rankings usually stay flat until then.
F01-17.F01-17-d2: Focus on link building, since technical and content work is done once.
F01-17.F01-17-d3: Add every structured data type available, whatever the page content.

F02-01.F02-01-d1: Google indexes submitted URLs first, then crawls them when someone searches.
F02-01.F02-01-d2: Google crawls the web at query time and ranks whatever pages it fetches.
F02-01.F02-01-d3: Google finds pages through sitemaps, indexes all of them, then ranks by backlinks.

F02-02.F02-02-d1: Discovery is fetching a URL, and crawling is adding it to the index.
F02-02.F02-02-d2: Discovery happens in Search Console, while crawling happens through links.
F02-02.F02-02-d3: Both are the same step, since Google fetches a URL as soon as it finds it.

F02-03.F02-03-d1: Through a sitemap submission, since Google doesn't follow internal links to new URLs.
F02-03.F02-03-d2: Through the Indexing API, which is the standard route for any new page.
F02-03.F02-03-d3: Through social shares, which Google can use as its main discovery source.

F02-04.F02-04-d1: Google reads the raw HTML and skips scripts, so JavaScript content is unseen.
F02-04.F02-04-d2: Google runs JavaScript with an older Chrome version that lacks modern features.
F02-04.F02-04-d3: Google can run JavaScript, but only for sites that are verified in Search Console.

F02-05.F02-05-d1: Marked with a noindex tag, which tells Googlebot to skip fetching it.
F02-05.F02-05-d2: Lacking backlinks from other sites, which Google requires before a first crawl.
F02-05.F02-05-d3: Missing a canonical tag, so Google can't decide whether to fetch it.

F02-06.F02-06-d1: They can make Google crawl more often to check whether the page has recovered.
F02-06.F02-06-d2: Google treats them as 404s and drops the URL at the first one.
F02-06.F02-06-d3: Google caches the last good version, so a 500 has no effect on crawling.

F02-07.F02-07-d1: Google saves the raw HTML of each crawled page without analyzing it.
F02-07.F02-07-d2: Google assigns each page a fixed ranking position for its main keyword.
F02-07.F02-07-d3: Google picks the page with the most backlinks and discards its duplicates for good.

F02-08.F02-08-d1: The URL the site owner marks with a canonical tag, which Google must follow.
F02-08.F02-08-d2: The oldest URL in a group of similar pages, which Google keeps as the original.
F02-08.F02-08-d3: The URL in a cluster with the most backlinks, which Google uses to pool rankings.

F02-09.F02-09-d1: Missing from the sitemap, which Google requires before indexing a page.
F02-09.F02-09-d2: A missing meta description, which Google needs before indexing a page.
F02-09.F02-09-d3: A URL that is too long or has parameters, which Google won't index.

F02-10.F02-10-d1: Google may still be testing it, since indexed pages wait a month before ranking.
F02-10.F02-10-d2: Its title lacks the exact keyword, which ranking requires.
F02-10.F02-10-d3: It is sandboxed, since new pages can't rank until the domain is a year old.

F02-11.F02-11-d1: Google rotates rankings at random to test click-through rates.
F02-11.F02-11-d2: Logged-in users see results ranked by their own past clicks rather than relevance.
F02-11.F02-11-d3: The results only differ when one searcher is using a VPN or private mode.

F02-12.F02-12-d1: Features depend on the schema the top pages use.
F02-12.F02-12-d2: Google rotates features on a schedule to test which ones users click.
F02-12.F02-12-d3: Google picks features based on the site's own preference in Search Console.

F02-13.F02-13-d1: Payment can't buy rankings, but Google Ads customers get crawled faster.
F02-13.F02-13-d2: Large advertisers get a dedicated rep who can request faster crawling.
F02-13.F02-13-d3: Only Google Partners can pay for faster indexing.

F02-14.F02-14-d1: Agree, since a submitted URL ranks once Google finishes processing it.
F02-14.F02-14-d2: Explain that ranking follows once the URL is indexed, which usually takes a few days.
F02-14.F02-14-d3: Resubmit the URL daily until it appears, since repeat requests raise priority.

F03-01.F03-01-d1: Check word count, keyword coverage, and readability scores against top results.
F03-01.F03-01-d2: Check the page's SEO tool score and how often it has been updated.
F03-01.F03-01-d3: Check time on page and bounce rate, since Google ranks by these metrics.

F03-03.F03-03-d1: It is a direct factor that Google scores from author bios and credentials.
F03-03.F03-03-d2: It is only a rater concept and has no link to how Google ranks pages.
F03-03.F03-03-d3: It is a sitewide score that Google can calculate and show in Search Console.

F03-04.F03-04-d1: Expert authorship is required on every page, whatever the topic.
F03-04.F03-04-d2: Experience can replace expertise, even for medical or financial advice.
F03-04.F03-04-d3: A named byline is what counts, since Google doesn't weigh expertise by topic.

F03-05.F03-05-d1: Sites that sell products, where checkout security counts more than content.
F03-05.F03-05-d2: News and current events topics, where freshness counts more than accuracy.
F03-05.F03-05-d3: Topics with high search volume, where Google can require expert schema.

F03-06.F03-06-d1: Rater scores feed directly into the ranking of each page they review.
F03-06.F03-06-d2: Raters can demote weak pages on topics they review.
F03-06.F03-06-d3: Raters can issue manual actions when a page fails their guidelines.

F03-07.F03-07-d1: Writing for trending queries first, then adapting the page for its audience.
F03-07.F03-07-d2: Writing in a conversational tone with the reader's keywords in every heading.
F03-07.F03-07-d3: Writing longer pages so visitors stay on the site and dwell time goes up.

F03-08.F03-08-d1: Outbound links to competitors, long paragraphs, and no keyword in the URL.
F03-08.F03-08-d2: Pages under 300 words, few images, and posting less than once a week.
F03-08.F03-08-d3: Missing author photos, no FAQ section, and dates left unchanged for a year.

F03-09.F03-09-d1: Pruning old pages raises the site's average freshness, which lifts rankings.
F03-09.F03-09-d2: Only pages older than two years should be deleted to gain a freshness boost.
F03-09.F03-09-d3: Changing publish dates can give the same freshness boost without deleting pages.

F03-10.F03-10-d1: Check third-party visibility scores first, since they show the cause.
F03-10.F03-10-d2: Look for a manual action, since content drops usually come from penalties.
F03-10.F03-10-d3: Update publish dates sitewide and wait for a recrawl.

F03-11.F03-11-d1: The text that appears above the fold, excluding tabs and user reviews.
F03-11.F03-11-d2: Any text written by the site owner, while tools and reviews count as supplementary.
F03-11.F03-11-d3: The longest block of text on the page, plus its headings and images.

F03-12.F03-12-d2: Expertise, originality, freshness, and depth of coverage.
F03-12.F03-12-d3: Expertise, readability, talent or skill, and accuracy.

F03-13.F03-13-d1: Attribution makes a summary original when each claim links to its source.
F03-13.F03-13-d2: Citing sources is enough if the summary is reworded to pass AI detectors.
F03-13.F03-13-d3: Summaries can be original when they cite more sources than competitors.

F03-14.F03-14-d1: Tabbed content counts as supplementary, so key specs belong above the fold.
F03-14.F03-14-d2: Tabbed content is given less weight, so it can't count as main content.
F03-14.F03-14-d3: Specs count as main content only in a plain table without tabs.

F03-15.F03-15-d1: Add review schema with star ratings and a summary of the product's main specs.
F03-15.F03-15-d2: Use a well-known expert's name as the byline, even if staff did the testing.
F03-15.F03-15-d3: Summarize manufacturer specs and customer ratings from major retailers.

F03-16.F03-16-d1: Label every page that used AI at any stage with Google's required tag.
F03-16.F03-16-d2: Avoid AI disclosures, since Google can read them as low quality.
F03-16.F03-16-d3: Use the AI label in Search Console, which Google shows next to results.

F03-17.F03-17-d1: They can help if the author bios list real-sounding credentials.
F03-17.F03-17-d2: They are fine as long as the content itself is accurate.
F03-17.F03-17-d3: They help, since Google rewards pages that show an author photo.

F04-01.F04-01-d1: AI features use a separate index, so SEO needs a different approach.
F04-01.F04-01-d2: AI answers come from model training data, so rankings no longer matter.
F04-01.F04-01-d3: AI features cite pages by brand mentions, so link-based SEO no longer applies.

F04-02.F04-02-d1: It retrains the model on new pages each week so answers stay current.
F04-02.F04-02-d2: It ranks pages by how closely their text matches the model's training data.
F04-02.F04-02-d3: It pulls answers from a separate AI index built from llms.txt files.

F04-03.F04-03-d1: Creating a separate page for each related query a model might search.
F04-03.F04-03-d2: The model spreads a query across several AI tools and merges their answers.
F04-03.F04-03-d3: Google merges related queries into one result page to save processing.

F04-04.F04-04-d1: Content about niche topics with low search volume and little competition.
F04-04.F04-04-d2: Content that combines the top-ranking pages into one longer summary.
F04-04.F04-04-d3: Content written by a person rather than generated with AI tools.

F04-05.F04-05-d1: It must use AI-specific schema and be listed in the site's llms.txt file.
F04-05.F04-05-d2: It needs to be indexed and rank in the top ten for the user's query.
F04-05.F04-05-d3: It needs a FAQ or HowTo schema block and a page speed score above 90.

F04-06.F04-06-d1: It is optional, but Google uses it to choose pages for AI Overviews.
F04-06.F04-06-d2: Google reads it like robots.txt to decide what its AI features can use.
F04-06.F04-06-d3: It is needed for AI Mode, but regular results ignore it.

F04-07.F04-07-d1: Google can only extract passages that sit under their own H2.
F04-07.F04-07-d2: AI features cite each page for one topic and ignore the rest of it.
F04-07.F04-07-d3: Short chunks of about 100 words are the format AI systems prefer.

F04-08.F04-08-d1: FAQPage schema is required for a page to appear in AI Overviews.
F04-08.F04-08-d2: Google uses a speakable-style AI markup to pick supporting links.
F04-08.F04-08-d3: Standard schema.org markup is a requirement for appearing in AI features.

F04-09.F04-09-d1: It can work, since AI features favor sites with more matching pages.
F04-09.F04-09-d2: It is fine if each page targets a different fan-out query.
F04-09.F04-09-d3: Scaled content rules apply to classic results, not to AI features.

F04-10.F04-10-d1: Validation errors can keep a page out of AI features until they're fixed.
F04-10.F04-10-d2: Semantic tags are how AI systems find answers, so they decide visibility.
F04-10.F04-10-d3: Markup doesn't matter, as AI features read only the page's plain text.

F04-11.F04-11-d1: Publish AI-written product pages at scale to cover fan-out queries.
F04-11.F04-11-d2: Add product schema with an AI tag, since feeds aren't used in AI answers.
F04-11.F04-11-d3: Enable all optional merchant programs, since each one is a ranking factor.

F04-12.F04-12-d1: Use Google Analytics referral data, which lists AI Overviews citations.
F04-12.F04-12-d2: Track citations with a rank tracker, since Google can't report AI visibility.
F04-12.F04-12-d3: Filter the standard Performance report by the AI Overviews search appearance.

F04-13.F04-13-d1: Add a noai meta tag, which Google reads as a sitewide opt-out from AI features.
F04-13.F04-13-d2: Block Google-Extended, which removes pages from AI Overviews and AI Mode.
F04-13.F04-13-d3: Turning off AI features in Search Console also drops pages from regular results.

F04-14.F04-14-d1: They replace SEO, since AI answers use different ranking signals.
F04-14.F04-14-d2: They require separate AI schema and an llms.txt file.
F04-14.F04-14-d3: They mean writing for chatbots, so pages no longer need to rank in Search.

F04-15.F04-15-d1: AI crawlers building a separate index for AI Overviews to draw on.
F04-15.F04-15-d2: An AI ranking mode where pages earn a score for agent compatibility.
F04-15.F04-15-d3: Chatbots that site owners add to pages to answer visitor questions.

F05-01.F05-01-d1: It bans AI text but allows AI-assisted images and outlines.
F05-01.F05-01-d2: It allows AI content as long as each page is labeled as AI-generated.
F05-01.F05-01-d3: It can detect AI text and usually ranks it below human writing.

F05-02.F05-02-d1: Using AI to write pages at all, whatever value they add for users.
F05-02.F05-02-d2: Publishing more than a set number of pages per day on one site.
F05-02.F05-02-d3: Using one template for many product pages that each list different specs.

F05-03.F05-03-d1: Review is needed to remove patterns that Google flags as AI-written.
F05-03.F05-03-d2: Models only err on recent events, so older facts need no checking.
F05-03.F05-03-d3: Human edits can lift a page above Google's AI-content threshold.

F05-04.F05-04-d1: Headings, internal links, and the URL slug of each page.
F05-04.F05-04-d2: Meta keywords, author bios, and the sitemap's priority values.
F05-04.F05-04-d3: Canonical tags, hreflang tags, and robots.txt rules.

F05-05.F05-05-d1: Publish it once it passes the Rich Results Test, since that checks accuracy.
F05-05.F05-05-d2: Add extra properties beyond the page content to qualify for more features.
F05-05.F05-05-d3: Keep it out of the page, since Google detects and ignores generated JSON-LD.

F05-06.F05-06-d1: A standard AI label on each page, in the format Google requires.
F05-06.F05-06-d2: No disclosure, since Google can treat it as a low-quality signal.
F05-06.F05-06-d3: The name of the AI model and prompt used, listed in the page's schema.

F05-07.F05-07-d1: An alt attribute that states the image was created with AI.
F05-07.F05-07-d2: A visible watermark saying 'AI-generated' placed in a corner of the image.
F05-07.F05-07-d3: Embedded EXIF metadata naming the AI tool used as the camera model.

F05-08.F05-08-d1: Via the standard title and description fields, with 'AI' added to the text.
F05-08.F05-08-d2: Via a product_ai_content flag set to true in the feed's custom labels.
F05-08.F05-08-d3: Via the description field only, since titles can't be AI-generated.

F05-09.F05-09-d1: They list the signals Google weights most, in order of importance.
F05-09.F05-09-d2: They spell out the rating criteria a page has to meet to rank first.
F05-09.F05-09-d3: Rater scores can move a page up once enough raters agree on it.

F06-01.F06-01-d1: robots.txt handles indexing, while noindex handles crawling.
F06-01.F06-01-d2: robots.txt removes pages from results, while noindex hides them from users.
F06-01.F06-01-d3: Both stop indexing, but robots.txt can work faster for large sections.

F06-02.F06-02-d1: Blocking it is fine, since Google can render pages from HTML alone.
F06-02.F06-02-d2: Blocking CSS frees crawl budget, which usually goes to more important pages.
F06-02.F06-02-d3: Block only the largest files, since small CSS doesn't use crawl budget.

F06-03.F06-03-d1: Google treats changefreq as a hint and uses priority to order crawling.
F06-03.F06-03-d2: Google follows changefreq for crawling but ignores lastmod, which sites often misuse.
F06-03.F06-03-d3: Google ignores lastmod but can use changefreq to plan recrawls.

F06-04.F06-04-d1: Use 302 for a permanent move, and 301 for a temporary one.
F06-04.F06-04-d2: Use 302 for both, since 301s pass less ranking signal.
F06-04.F06-04-d3: Use 301 for moves within a site and 302 for moves to a new domain.

F06-05.F06-05-d1: A 404 page with a custom design instead of the default server page.
F06-05.F06-05-d2: A page that returns 404 but is still linked from other pages.
F06-05.F06-05-d3: A temporary 404 that Google retries before treating the page as removed.

F06-06.F06-06-d1: Redirect all old URLs to the new homepage, then submit the new sitemap.
F06-06.F06-06-d2: Use 302 redirects during the move, then switch them to 301s a year later.
F06-06.F06-06-d3: Point canonical tags at the new domain, since they can replace redirects in a move.

F06-07.F06-07-d1: Rely on scroll events, since Googlebot scrolls like a user.
F06-07.F06-07-d2: Load more items on scroll and list the first page in the sitemap.
F06-07.F06-07-d3: Use #fragment URLs for each section so Google can index them.

F06-08.F06-08-d1: rel=next and rel=prev are required so Google can group the pages.
F06-08.F06-08-d2: Each page needs a canonical pointing to page one of the set.
F06-08.F06-08-d3: All pages need to be merged into a view-all page for crawling.

F06-09.F06-09-d1: When a site has more than a few hundred pages, whatever its crawl stats.
F06-09.F06-09-d2: When Search Console reports any URL as discovered but not indexed.
F06-09.F06-09-d3: When rankings drop after a core update, as crawl budget affects quality scores.

F06-10.F06-10-d1: Canonicalize each translation to the main language version.
F06-10.F06-10-d2: Redirect each visitor by IP to their own language.
F06-10.F06-10-d3: Use the lang attribute, which Google relies on to pick versions.

F06-11.F06-11-d1: Product detail URLs, since category pages already list their content.
F06-11.F06-11-d2: Paginated category URLs, such as page 2 and beyond of a listing.
F06-11.F06-11-d3: Out-of-stock product URLs, until the items are available again.

F06-12.F06-12-d1: It does once Google recrawls the page after the markup passes tests.
F06-12.F06-12-d2: It guarantees display for most markup types, though reviews need approval.
F06-12.F06-12-d3: It can, but only if the site has enough authority to be trusted.

F06-13.F06-13-d1: Video, podcasts, product reviews, local businesses, and news.
F06-13.F06-13-d2: Images, recipes, product reviews, job postings, and medical content.
F06-13.F06-13-d3: Articles, podcasts, AI content, apps, and news.

F06-14.F06-14-d1: PageSpeed Insights shows site-wide data, while CWV tests single pages.
F06-14.F06-14-d2: CWV measures lab data only, while PageSpeed Insights shows field data alone.
F06-14.F06-14-d3: They report the same data, but CWV can be used to request recrawls.

F06-15.F06-15-d1: Add a meta keywords tag and a longer meta description.
F06-15.F06-15-d2: Add every schema type that could apply, even if not on the page.
F06-15.F06-15-d3: Write a longer title tag, since Google shows more of it on mobile.

F07-01.F07-01-d1: Google sees a cached copy that can be weeks older than your version.
F07-01.F07-01-d2: Google usually skips content that loads more than a second after the HTML.
F07-01.F07-01-d3: Your browser shows the desktop page, while Google sees only the AMP version.

F07-02.F07-02-d1: A button with an onclick handler that loads the page's URL.
F07-02.F07-02-d2: An <a> tag with a #fragment href that loads the page's content.
F07-02.F07-02-d3: A link with the keyword repeated in its title attribute.

F07-03.F07-03-d1: One URL is fine if the shell has good metadata.
F07-03.F07-03-d2: Pre-rendering the home page is enough for the whole app.
F07-03.F07-03-d3: Hash-based routes are enough, since Google can tell those screens apart.

F07-04.F07-04-d1: Tests check page speed, which decides whether Google runs the scripts.
F07-04.F07-04-d2: Google runs JavaScript only in a second wave that can take months.
F07-04.F07-04-d3: Testing is mostly needed for sites that still use old jQuery libraries.

F07-05.F07-05-d1: Change the publish date on updated pages so Google sees new content.
F07-05.F07-05-d2: Ping Google with each update, which triggers an immediate recrawl.
F07-05.F07-05-d3: Use the Indexing API for all page types so Google sees updates.

F07-06.F07-06-d1: Google can't load more than a few images per page while crawling.
F07-06.F07-06-d2: Image-heavy pages load slowly, which usually blocks them from indexing.

C03-05.C03-05-d2: Large sitemaps, hreflang annotations, canonical tags and image galleries.
